extracted.intended_audience: managers, AI/UX designers, and researchers studying consumer–AI interactions (marketing scholars, product managers, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing AI-enabled consumer experiences (classification, delegation, and social interactions) that avoid bias, preserve self-efficacy, and minimize consumer alienation. Includes organizational, experience-design, and research recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational learning to surface and address biased treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should learn how to surface and address accounts of biased treatment arising from classification errors and other AI-driven decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike data-capture errors, classification errors produce near-term signals across different parts of an organization; firms must examine marketing and consumer-facing departments and their taken-for-granted assumptions about whom they serve. Learn about specific biases present in company algorithms and processes, collaborate with computer scientists, sociologists, and psychologists, and share audit processes and outcomes (including through lobbying) to ensure regulation protects consumers from discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic audits for inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms should assess AI systems for risks of inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions and reasonably address the results of such assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively conduct audits (in the spirit of the Algorithmic Accountability Act) with technology experts and thought leaders; make audits regular, transparent where appropriate, and institute protocols to react swiftly to any bias uncovered (Zou and Schiebinger 2018). Share audit processes and outcomes to inform policy and stakeholder trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience design to minimize consumers feeling misunderstood
rubrics_metrics.description: Design AI classification experiences so consumers’ likelihood of feeling misunderstood is minimized (e.g., diversify content and broaden product suggestions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build on consumer listening to diversify and broaden the content provided and propose products dissimilar from the user’s preference profile (example: Spotify’s Taste Breakers). Experiment to avoid overfitting to past short-term behaviors which can ignore long-term goals and increase polarization; periodically ask consumers to validate AI-based inferences to increase satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable user validation and participatory updating of AI inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer consumers opportunities to validate and update the AI’s view of themselves to reduce frustration and increase satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater user participation in algorithm implementation increases satisfaction; periodically offering updates of inferred categorizations can reduce feelings of being misunderstood and improve acceptance of decision-support systems (Wierenga and Oude Ophuis 1997; Dietvorst et al. 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify hiring and representation throughout design and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure hiring and organizational culture include members of social minority groups and people with disabilities to identify and eliminate biases in AI design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diverse viewpoints at all stages of AI classification experience design (including employees with disabilities to eliminate disability bias). Collaborate with non-technical disciplines (sociology, psychology, linguistics, critical theory, humanities) to avoid ideological blind spots and harmful stereotypes in product design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute protocols for rapid organizational response to identified bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When audits or consumer reports uncover bias, firms should have protocols to swiftly react and remediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swift reactions are necessary; organizational learning should ensure that insights from audits and consumer listening permeate firm culture (technical and non-technical functions) so remediation and process changes follow quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design delegation experiences to protect self-efficacy and identity
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI performs tasks on consumers’ behalf, design the delegation experience to preserve consumers’ sense of accomplishment, self-efficacy, and agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use division of labor to let consumers retain tasks that are intrinsically motivating; allow small amounts of control (e.g., the ability to correct or slightly adjust algorithm outputs) which can increase acceptance of superior algorithms. Ask consumers which activities they prefer to reserve versus delegate, and design interfaces that support that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide small, tangible controls to re-establish agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer small controls or corrective actions in AI interactions that re-establish consumers’ sense of control and competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even minimal acts (e.g., allowing a user to correct an algorithm’s output) can re-establish self-worth and increase adoption of algorithmic decisions (Marks 2005; Dietvorst et al. 2016). For example, allow peripheral customizations in autonomous vehicles and the option to correct outputs in digital assistants or recommendation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design human–AI supervision structures for high-stakes domains
rubrics_metrics.description: In domains like medicine or safety-critical systems, design the structure of human supervision over AI to maintain trust and protect outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For surgical robots and other high-stakes applications, the way surgeon or human supervision is structured is central to success; design interfaces and workflows that maintain appropriate human oversight and patient trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and operationalize alienation and its causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect data to detect and measure consumer alienation with social AI experiences (e.g., operationalize using stress measures in customers’ voices) and use those measurements to improve systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage technology to gauge and measure alienation (amount of stress, conversational breakdowns) in chats and voice interactions; combine quantitative measures with qualitative consumer interviews and consultations with psychologists, gerontologists, and sociologists to develop generalizable insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphism that perpetuates harmful stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure anthropomorphic design choices do not reproduce or calcify harmful social stereotypes (e.g., gendered or racialized defaults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disseminate information across the organization about societal consequences of subservient or gendered AI personas; involve linguists, critical theorists, and social psychologists in design decisions. Consider default voice/name choices carefully and move away from using female names/voices as defaults to reduce reinforcement of stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider less humanlike designs to reduce alienation and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts, making AI less humanlike may avoid perpetuating stereotypes and reduce alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows that less humanlike AI may avoid invoking harmful social dynamics; balance benefits of anthropomorphism (trust, natural interaction) against risks of exclusion and stereotype reinforcement (Hadi et al. 2020).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize interactions and provide clear explanations when failures occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalize AI social interactions (use customer’s name) and explain reasons for malfunctions to reduce alienation and improve acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumers respond positively to personalization and to explanations for errors; firms should also ensure easy and swift transitions from AI to human representatives when interactions become difficult or aversive (Hart, Heskett, and Sasser 1990; Carmon et al. 2020).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and learn from consumers who experience alienation or exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly solicit information from consumers who experienced alienation or exclusion by AI to inform corrective design and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with affected consumers, include their perspectives in organizational learning, and use those insights to modify algorithms, interfaces, and service pathways (example: Universal Credit failures for people with disabilities). Involve cross-disciplinary experts to understand causes and consequences.
